name: Colloidal sulfur

lead: Colloidal sulfur is sulfur in very fine, suspended form. In skin care it appears in spot treatments and masks aimed at pimples and congested skin, where it acts as a keratolytic, loosening dead surface cells.
Sulfur has a long history in skin care; the Ebers Papyrus records an ancient Egyptian sulfur ointment for eyelid conditions.

paras: People apply sulfur-containing spot treatments or masks to blemished areas for a set time and rinse; products state their own directions.
Sulfur can dry or irritate skin and smells strongly; people with sensitive skin or sulfa allergy consult product labels or clinicians.

label.generic: SODIUM LAURETH SULFAT,DECYL GLUCOSIDE,PALM KERNELAMIDE DEA,COCAMIDOPROPYL BETAINE,LONICERA JAPONICA(HONEYSUCKLE) FLOWER EXTRACT,COLLOIDAL SULFUR.

chain: Loosens dead skin cells and dries blemishes
angle.text: Applied to blemishes in spot treatments, sulfur is used to dry spots and exfoliate the surface so skin looks clearer.

lead: Colloidal sulfur is elemental sulfur dispersed in a fine suspension. In skin care it is used in spot treatments and masks as a keratolytic, a substance that helps loosen dead skin cells, with the aim of clearer-looking skin.

Sulfur has been used on skin since antiquity: the Ebers Papyrus describes an Egyptian sulfur ointment used for granular eyelids.[1] Most scientific literature on colloidal sulfur concerns other fields, such as medical imaging tracers and wastewater chemistry, rather than cosmetic use.

paras: The Ebers Papyrus records a sulfur ointment used by ancient Egyptians for granular eyelids.[1]
Colloidal sulfur appears in spot masks as a keratolytic ingredient in products aimed at blemishes.
No studies found for colloidal sulfur as a cosmetic spot treatment. Published items using the term concern unrelated fields such as radiolabelled transit studies and water treatment.
